name: Low & No Alcohol
tagline: Kombucha, kefir, shrubs, de-alcoholised wine, botanical waters, and more. A fast-growing space where the Good Food Standard matters most.

learn.how_we_evaluate: This category spans ancient fermented traditions and very new production methods. We look at what's actually in the bottle, how it was made, and whether the label tells the truth — particularly on ABV, residual sugar, and origin of botanical ingredients. For de-alcoholised wine, we evaluate the base wine quality and the de-alcoholisation method. For fermented drinks, we look at fermentation time, sugar content, and ingredient origin.
what_to_look_for: Precise ABV stated — 0.0% and <0.5% are meaningfully different
Named botanical, tea, or grape ingredients with origin where possible
Residual sugar disclosed — especially important for de-alcoholised wine
Fermentation method explained for kombucha, kefir, kvass
Vegan certification for de-alcoholised wine (conventional fining agents)
red_flags: ABV stated only as 'less than 0.5%' with no more precision for 0.0% products
Added sugar not disclosed or buried in small print
Generic botanical names with no origin
Equivalence claims — 'tastes just like wine' used to avoid honest description

key_terms.definition: 0.0% means no detectable alcohol (below 0.05% ABV under EU rules). <0.5% means trace alcohol — the same level found in some fruit juices and ripe bananas. The difference is real and meaningful for people who avoid alcohol for religious, medical, or personal reasons.

Symbiotic Culture of Bacteria and Yeast. The live culture used to ferment kombucha. A kombucha made with a live, well-maintained SCOBY is fundamentally different from a carbonated tea with kombucha flavouring.

A gentle de-alcoholisation technology that uses centrifugal force and low temperature to separate alcohol from wine while preserving aromatics. Considered superior to vacuum distillation for maintaining wine character.
